about.section02P1Post: — is a form of long-distance cycling where the rider must complete a set distance within a time limit. It's not a race. There is no winner.
about.section02P2: There are only riders who reach the finish — and riders who try again.
about.section02P3Post: — and beyond — every brevet is a personal challenge against the route, the weather and yourself.
about.section03P1: The GRC Platform was born from the need of a community that deserves better tools. A place where every rider can find the season's brevets, track their history and see years of progress in the saddle.
about.section03P2: The platform doesn't belong to any company. It was built by a rider, for riders — with respect for the culture of Randonneuring and love for the Greek countryside we cross every year.

cop31Banner.title: 🚴 COP31 Bike Ride — the Greek leg:
cop31Banner.activeText: happening right now, Athens → Turkey, cycling for the climate.

cop31.metaTitle: COP31 Bike Ride — Greek Leg | GRC
cop31.metaDescription: Greece is joining the global COP31 Bike Ride relay. From Athens to the Turkish border, 30/9–7/10, coordinated by the Hellenic Autonomous Randonneurs.
cop31.heroSubtitle: The Greek leg: from Athens to the Turkish border
cop31.section01Heading: What is the COP31 Bike Ride
cop31.section01P1: The COP31 Bike Ride is the largest bicycle relay ever attempted, aiming to put everyday cycling on the map as a quick-win solution for cutting greenhouse gas emissions. It set off from Belém, Brazil, host city of the previous COP, and carries its message through a chain of connected routes all the way to Antalya, Turkey.
cop31.section01P2: Across Europe, parallel cycling legs are unfolding country by country, with thousands of cyclists, local communities, cities and organizations taking part. The idea is simple: the bicycle becomes the thread that connects people and places around a shared message of sustainable mobility, environmental protection and climate action.
cop31.section00P: COP31 is the 31st United Nations Climate Change Conference, the global summit where countries from around the world negotiate joint action against the climate crisis. It will be held in Antalya, Turkey, from November 9 to 20, 2026.
cop31.section02P1: This year, at the last minute, the Greek cycling community joined the global relay too. Coordination of the Greek leg has been taken on by the Hellenic Autonomous Randonneurs (HAR), with one core goal: Greek participation shouldn't be the work of a single club, but a joint effort of the entire Greek cycling community — clubs, groups and independent cyclists alike.
cop31.section02P2: We set off from Athens on September 30. Over eight days we'll cross Greece by bicycle, reaching Pınarhisar, Turkey on October 7, where the Greek leg joins the continuation of the international route.
cop31.routeIntro: These are the main daily stops — the real route runs through everything in between them too. Detailed GPX tracks for each day will be published progressively. Total distance: approximately 1,300 km.
cop31.joinP1: You don't need to ride the whole route. You can join for a single day, for part of a stage, or even just a few kilometres when the relay passes through your area. Everyone is equal and everyone is welcome: athletes, randonneurs, people who cycle every day, groups of friends out for a ride, and anyone who simply loves to cycle.
cop31.joinP2: Detailed GPX tracks for each day will be published progressively, so cyclists from every city, town or village the relay passes through can see exactly where it goes and come out to meet it on the road.
cop31.joinP3: It doesn't matter whether it's 100, 50, 20 or 5 kilometres. What matters is that, from Athens to the border, we build one big Greek cycling relay together.
cop31.supportP1: The effort is also developing at an institutional level: outreach has already begun with public bodies, Regions and Municipalities across the country, aiming for public Letters of Commitment in support of the initiative's goals. The Greek leg will also be covered in the media and on social media.
cop31.supportSponsor: With the kind support of Seanergy Maritime Holdings Corp. — Official Supporter of COP31 Bike Ride – Greek Branch.
cop31.seanergyChipTitle: How is Seanergy connected to the message of COP31?
cop31.seanergyP1: The transition to a more sustainable future isn't about a single sector. It's about how we move around our cities, how we travel, how we produce and use energy — and how people and goods are transported across the entire world.
cop31.seanergyP2: That's why it matters to us that Seanergy Maritime Holdings Corp. supports the Greek leg of the COP31 Bike Ride as Official Supporter. As part of the international and European drive toward shipping decarbonization and net-zero emissions by 2050, Seanergy is pursuing targeted interventions grounded in technical study, evaluation of real performance data, and systematic exploration of available solutions, aiming for continuous improvement in energy efficiency and a smaller environmental footprint for its fleet.
cop31.seanergyP3: A key part of this strategy is fleet renewal, through investment in newer vessels and orders for new, high energy-efficiency ships.
cop31.seanergyP4: At the same time, the company carries out targeted energy upgrades on its existing vessels and makes use of digital systems for monitoring and optimizing energy performance.
cop31.seanergyP5: Seanergy also makes use of sustainable biofuels, having by now built up substantial operational experience in using and managing them. A notable part of this effort is its participation in the European research programme SAFeCRAFT, which develops and evaluates solutions for using hydrogen on an existing vessel in its fleet — contributing to technologies that can support the decarbonization of shipping.
cop31.seanergyP6: From sustainable mobility in our cities to the decarbonization of shipping, the transition requires technological innovation, collaboration, and continuous progress.
cop31.seanergyThanks: We thank Seanergy Maritime Holdings Corp. for supporting the Greek mission.
cop31.linkFacebookNote: The event's discussion tab lists the Municipalities that have expressed support for the initiative.
cop31.linkPdf: HAR's official call to cycling clubs (PDF)
cop31.linkSeanergy: Seanergy Maritime Holdings Corp. — official website
cop31.footerQuote: The COP31 Bike Ride doesn't belong to one club, one team, or one category of cyclist. It belongs to everyone.

randonneuring.metaDescription: The history of randonneuring from its origins to today: ACP, UAF, LRM, Provence Randonneurs, Paris-Brest-Paris, and the global structure of brevets.
randonneuring.heroSubtitle: Ultra-distance cycling isn't just an endurance sport — it's a living tradition with over a century of history, full of splits, commercial rivalries, and institutions that shaped what we do today.
randonneuring.section1P1: The terms Randonneuring, Randonnée and Randonneur come from French and mean "long tour/journey". In cycling, they describe riding long distances in full self-supported (unsupported) conditions, within specific time limits, but with no competitive element — there's no ranking or winner.
randonneuring.section1Note: 💡 Legal note: The term "Randonneuring" is a common descriptive French word — it isn't a trademark of any club.
randonneuring.timeline1Body: The newspaper Le Petit Journal organizes the first PBP as a brutal professional race — 1,200 km with no checkpoints, no support. It's held every 10 years because of how grueling it is.
randonneuring.timeline2Body: On November 30, 1904, the Audax Club Parisien is founded in Paris. That same year, Henri Desgrange — editor of the newspaper L'Auto and founder of the Tour de France — organizes the first 200 km brevet in the Audax style: riders move as a single group at a fixed average speed of 18 km/h, led by a "road captain". In 1906, Desgrange formally hands ACP the management of these brevets.
randonneuring.timeline3Title: The Great Split — Birth of "Allure Libre"
randonneuring.timeline3Intro: A double conflict upends everything: ACP partners with L'Auto's commercial rival, and is accused of breaching the fixed 18 km/h pace. An enraged Desgrange strips ACP of its Audax rights.
randonneuring.timeline3Item1: Those loyal to Desgrange leave and found (April 1922) the Union des Audax Clubs Parisiens (UACP), renamed on January 1, 1956 to Union des Audax Français (UAF). They keep the group-pace style to this day.
randonneuring.timeline3Item2: ACP, on September 11, 1921, organizes the first Brevet de Randonneur à Allure Libre — free pace, no leaders or groups, as long as each rider finishes within the time limit. This is the format we ride today.
randonneuring.timeline4P1: At the 5th edition of PBP, ACP and UACP persuade Desgrange to allow a parallel amateur field. For the first time, three groups ride together: professionals, amateur Audax riders (group style, UAF), and amateur Randonneurs (allure libre, ACP).
randonneuring.timeline4P2: 1951 is the last year professionals race PBP — the Tour de France has become the undisputed king. In 1975 UAF discontinues its own group-style PBP for lack of participation. ACP remains the sole, undisputed organizer of PBP Randonneur.
randonneuring.timeline5P1: On August 26, 1983 — the day right after the 10th PBP — ACP, together with representatives from 8 countries, founds Les Randonneurs Mondiaux (LRM), randonneuring's global federation.
randonneuring.timeline5P2: Its purpose: LRM takes over the certification and oversight of Super Brevets (1200 km+ events) worldwide, leaving ACP with the classic BRM series (200-1000 km) and PBP. Notable LRM events: London–Edinburgh–London (LEL) in the UK, Rocky Mountain 1200 in Canada.
randonneuring.timeline6P1: Randonneuse Sophie Matter, living in Provence, seeks a format combining 600 km with at least 10,000 meters of climbing in fully self-supported conditions — something that doesn't yet exist in France. She presents the idea to ACP, which approves it and puts her solely in charge.
randonneuring.timeline6P2: This is how Super Randonnées (SR600) are born: permanent routes of 600 km / 10,000+ m of climbing, with no set start date, ridable any time.
randonneuring.timeline7Body: On November 7, 2011, Sophie Matter founds Provence Randonneurs in Carcès, southern France — a legal and organizational "home" to run her own extreme events. In 2012 the 1000 du Sud launches, an incredibly tough 1000 km route in the mountains of southern France.
randonneuring.timeline8Title: SR600 passes exclusively to Provence Randonneurs
randonneuring.timeline8P1: Weighed down by the bureaucratic load of the classic BRM series and PBP, ACP decides to step back from SR600. In December 2021, it formally hands Provence Randonneurs exclusive worldwide management, oversight, and certification of all SR600 routes. From 2022 onward, ACP withdraws from this area entirely.
randonneuring.timeline8P2: A small club founded by one passionate Randonneuse grows into a global institution.
randonneuring.section3Heading: 🗺️ The "Province" Concept — How the Sport Expanded
randonneuring.section3P1: In French, province means any region outside the Paris area (Île-de-France). ACP originally organized brevets exclusively around the capital. As the sport spread, it began licensing local clubs across the rest of France — the so-called Brevets des Provinces — while keeping central control and final certification (homologation) in Paris.
randonneuring.section3Quote: That same "Paris + province" model was applied as-is to the sport's international expansion. Each country was treated as a kind of "province": it has an official ACP Representative who collects local brevet results and sends them to Paris for the official homologation number.
randonneuring.section3Note: When you finish a 200 km brevet in Greece, your card travels (digitally) to Paris for official certification — continuing a tradition started by cyclists in the French provinces.
randonneuring.orgAcpDesc: The "parent" club. Manages the classic BRM series (200, 300, 400, 600, 1000 km) and Paris-Brest-Paris — the biggest ultra-distance cycling event in the world. Style: Allure Libre.
randonneuring.orgUafDesc: Independently maintains its own brevet series in France and Europe, exclusively in the group Audax style (fixed 18 km/h with a road captain) — the original format that ACP abandoned in 1921.
randonneuring.orgLrmDesc: The global federation. Oversees Super Brevets — 1200 km+ events outside PBP. Notable events: London–Edinburgh–London (LEL), Rocky Mountain 1200. Style: Allure Libre.
randonneuring.orgProvenceDesc: Sophie Matter's club — creator of SR600. Since 2022 it has exclusive worldwide management of Super Randonnées (SR600): permanent routes of 600 km / 10,000+ m of climbing, with no fixed start date.
randonneuring.ctaDesc: Bike, gear, training, nutrition, strategy & the Greek community
randonneuring.footerSources: Sources: ACP, LRM, Provence Randonneurs, Union des Audax Français

guide.metaDescription: A complete, practical guide to randonneuring: bike, gear, training, nutrition, strategy and the Greek community. From zero to your first 200.
guide.heroSubtitle: Crossing over into the world of brevets is a wonderful journey. Randonneuring isn't a race for speed — it's about endurance, self-sufficiency, smart energy management, and mental strength.
guide.section0P1: Before investing in gear or planning workouts, make sure your body is ready for the nature of this sport: long, continuous effort, often in harsh weather (heat, cold, rain), and at hours you'd normally be asleep.
guide.section0TipBold: A cardiac check-up once a year.
guide.section0TipBody: A stress test with a cardiologist is the bare minimum before you put your heart through such a prolonged effort. This isn't just for older riders — silent heart problems can exist at any age without ever showing up in everyday activity.
guide.section0P2: This becomes even more critical as you move up in distance (300, 400, 600 km), where the body operates for many hours under stress, with sleep deprivation and often extreme temperatures. Don't take your fitness for granted — get an annual medical clearance.
guide.section1P1: On brevets you'll spend anywhere from 8 to over 40 hours continuously in the saddle. You don't need an expensive carbon bike; you need something comfortable and reliable. One rule applies here: Comfort = Performance.
guide.bikeItem1Body: Ideal categories. They have a more upright geometry that eases strain on the back, neck and shoulders, and accept wider tires.
guide.bikeItem2Body: Allow lower pressures, absorb vibration, and dramatically reduce body fatigue with no noticeable loss of speed.
guide.bikeItem3Body: E.g. 50-34 up front with an 11-32 or 11-34 in the back. They'll save your legs on long climbs once fatigue has built up.
guide.subtitleBikeFit: Bike fit: the most critical step
guide.section1P2: A great bike set up wrong is worse than an average bike set up right. You usually find this out after some distance — say at 120 km — with pain that wasn't there at 40.
guide.fitItem1Body: Puts pressure on the front of the knee (patella). Also causes a rocking pedal stroke that wastes energy.
guide.fitItem2Body: Pain in the hip or back of the knee. Over long distances it can lead to tendinitis.
guide.fitItem3Body: Loads the neck and shoulders. After 5–6 hours of riding it turns into sharp neck pain.
guide.fitItem4Body: Knee pain from strain on the iliotibial band. Not reversible without adjusting the cleats and/or adding insoles.
guide.tipBikeFitBold: Get a bike fit from a specialized shop.
guide.tipBikeFitBody: It costs around €50–100 and is the best investment you can make — long before expensive shoes or a saddle. If you're shopping for a bike, don't buy blind without test-riding it. The wrong frame size and geometry will force you to buy another bike later.
guide.section2P1: The core principle: full self-sufficiency. You need to be prepared for any change in weather or mechanical issue without outside help.
guide.clothingItem1Body: The single most critical piece of gear. Invest in the best your budget allows.
guide.clothingItem2Body: Essential for preventing chafing and saddle sores after hours in the saddle. Applied before putting on the bib shorts.
guide.clothingItem3Body: Bib shorts are always worn with no underwear underneath. The chamois is designed to wick moisture away from the skin, while underwear traps it and adds seams — both increase the risk of saddle sores.
guide.clothingItem4Body: You might start a day cold and end up in the rain. Removable sleeves, leg warmers and a packable rain jacket are essential.
guide.subtitleSafety: Safety & self-sufficiency — mandatory by the rules
guide.safetyItem1Body: A very strong front light (with long battery life or the ability to recharge from a power bank) and at least two red rear lights (one steady, one blinking).
guide.safetyItem2Body: Mandatory for nighttime hours or low-visibility conditions.
guide.safetyItem3Body: 2–3 spare tubes, tire levers, pump, patches, multi-tool. You need to be able to change a tube quickly, even in the dark if needed.
guide.subtitleBags: Bags — carry the weight on the bike
guide.bagsItem1Body: For quick access on the move: food, phone, power bank.
guide.bagsItem2Body: For the clothes you shed, your repair kit and extra supplies. Forget backpacks — they cause sweating and shoulder pain.
guide.section3P1: Randonneuring doesn't require "talent". It requires endurance, energy management and organization — three things you build gradually, kilometer by kilometer.
guide.subtitleWhatItTakes: What does this kind of cycling take?
guide.section3P2: It's not just legs. It's lungs (aerobic capacity), pacing (not burning out early), proper hydration and fueling, planning your stops, and mental toughness once fatigue has piled up. The fastest rider doesn't win — the one who finishes does.
guide.startItem1Body: First rides — getting used to the saddle, the gear, your breathing rhythm.
guide.startItem2Body: You start to understand energy and hydration management.
guide.startItem3Body: The first big psychological barrier. If you clear it comfortably, you're on the right track.
guide.startItem4Body: The "dress rehearsal" for your first 200. If it feels good, you're ready.
guide.section3P3: For your first 200, no. The basics are simple: consistency with weekly rides and one long weekend ride that you build up gradually. A coach helps if you want to optimize, but it isn't a prerequisite.
guide.section4P1: Building up as a randonneur happens gradually, step by step. A healthy beginner who can already ride 40–50 km without trouble can move up a level by following this timeline.
guide.distance1Change: Managing a steady pace and continuous fueling.
guide.distance2Change: First experience riding in the dark.
guide.section5P1: You don't need to ride 200 km in training to finish your first 200. Training is built on consistency and building an aerobic base (Zone 2).
guide.planItem1Body: 1–2 short, steady rides (1.5–2 hours) at a pace where you can talk comfortably without gasping for air.
guide.planItem2Body: Your big ride of the week. Increase it by ~10% each week. Once you can complete a 130–140 km ride with comparable elevation, you're ready.
guide.subtitleElevation: The elevation you need to watch out for
guide.section5P2: Routes in Greece are rarely flat. As a general rule:
guide.tipElevation: Don't just look at total elevation gain — also check the maximum gradient of the climbs. Train on sustained 6–8% climbs to learn to keep your heart rate steady without blowing up.
guide.section5P3: The week before the brevet isn't a training week — it's a recovery week. This is called tapering: you drastically cut your mileage so you arrive at the start fresh.
guide.taperItem1Body: Maximum 30–40 km of easy riding, no climbs and no intensity.
guide.taperItem2Body: Ideally full rest, or 15–20 minutes of easy spinning to shake out the legs.
guide.taperItem3Body: Anxiety leads many riders to "squeeze in one more big ride" in that final week — it does more harm than good.
guide.section6P1: If you feel hungry or thirsty, your performance has already dropped and it's very hard to recover — what's called bonking. Fueling starts from minute one.
guide.food1Note: Bananas, bars, gels, dried fruit snacks, dried fruit
guide.food2Note: One bottle of water, one with electrolytes. Small sips every 15–20 minutes
guide.food3Note: After 4–5 hours your stomach wants something savory. Toast, potatoes, pasta
guide.section7P1: The time limit is 13.5 hours (including stops). An average moving speed of 20–22 km/h gives you plenty of margin.
guide.strategy1Title: Don't get swept up at the start
guide.strategy1Body: It's the most common mistake. You'll see groups taking off at 35+ km/h. Let them go. Find your own pace — one where you can talk without gasping for air.
guide.strategy2Body: Time is lost at the stops, not on the road. A 5-minute stop for a stamp and water is fine. A 45-minute coffee stop will let you cool down and eat into your buffer.
guide.strategy3Body: Don't think "I still have 150 km left". Think "I have 30 km to the next control, where I'll eat a banana". Mindset is what beats fatigue.
guide.section8P1: At the start you receive a card — the Brevet Card. It's the official proof of your participation. At every control point it gets stamped by a shop or café on the route, or by a volunteer from the organization. At the end, the organizer verifies the card and records your result.
guide.section8P2: Some control points have no stamp — instead you take a photo at a specific spot (e.g. a sign, a bridge, a church) as proof you passed through there. The timestamp on the photo on your phone verifies you were within the time limit.
guide.subtitleOutOfTime: If you run out of time
guide.section8P3: ACP's newer rules allow you to pass a control after its closing time by simply taking a photo as proof. However, if you finish outside the overall time limit, the brevet isn't officially recorded. You can still continue for personal satisfaction.
guide.subtitleStuck: If you get stuck along the way
guide.section8P4: Randonneuring is built on self-sufficiency — there's no official support to "pick you up" if you get stuck. In rare cases there may be a support vehicle from the organizer, but it's not something you can count on. Always have a plan B: either someone you can call to come get you, or finding a bus or other transport from where you are.
guide.subtitleClubRegistration: Do you need to join a club?
guide.section9P1: To take part in an official brevet and have your result recognized internationally or nationally, you need a registration number from one of the two official bodies in Greece:
guide.section9P2: Some clubs (e.g. Ble Cycling Club) also keep their own member registry for their own events (e.g. permanents) or group rides.
guide.section9P3: There's no fixed price. The cost of entering a brevet varies depending on distance and organizer.
guide.section9P4: For ΛΕ.Π.Ο.Τ.Ε. brevets, insurance is mandatory — without it you can't take part. For H.A.R. brevets it isn't required.
guide.section9P5: Getting to the start is entirely your own responsibility — it isn't provided by the organizer.
guide.section10P1: Randonneuring in Greece is remarkably well developed. All official events are internationally certified by Audax Club Parisien.
guide.club1Body: The official national body managing brevets in our country. Coordinates the central annual calendar for all organizers. Runs iconic brevets and the flagship Giro Central Greece (1,400 km).
guide.club2Body: A new, dynamic, nationwide community of ultra-distance organizers and riders. Focused on the authentic culture of self-sufficiency, exploring new routes, and a love of the journey.
guide.club3Body: Based in Athens (founded 2012), one of the most active crews in the scene. Introduced the institution of permanents (fixed routes you can ride any day) and organizes popular brevets across Greece.
guide.club4Body: Cycling Union of Veteran Athletes. Organizes some of the most massive, classic and polished brevets (mainly in Attica and the Peloponnese), serving as an ideal entry point for many new riders.
guide.regionalClubsBody: Excellent local groups organize brevets across the whole country — Greek Randonneurs, Ποδηλάτες Χίου, Γ.Σ. Λευκάδας, Φιλαθλητικός Όμιλος Πύργου, Π.Ο. Καρδίτσας, and others — showcasing the terrain and beauty of each region.
guide.tipFirstContactBody: Follow the groups on social media — that's where open rides and casual free rides get announced. Don't hesitate to say "I'm a beginner, I want to give it a try" — there will always be a group of experienced randonneurs happy to bring you along.
guide.checklist1: Bike check: correct tire pressure, clean & lubed chain, brakes in top condition.
guide.checklist2: Charge all devices: GPS / phone / front & rear lights / power bank.
guide.checklist3: Load the route (GPX file) onto your bike computer or phone.
guide.checklist4: Chamois cream applied before putting on your bib shorts.
guide.checklist5: Brevet Card in a waterproof ziploc bag.
guide.checklist6: Extra food in your pocket for the first hour (bar, banana, gel).
guide.checklist7: Reflective vest easily accessible — not at the bottom of your bag.
guide.footerCtaTitle: Good luck on your new journey!
guide.footerCtaBody: The feeling when you finish your first 200 and get that stamp is impossible to put into words.

harGuide.topic1ShortDesc: Independent Greek body for autonomous randonneuring
harGuide.topic1Content:
Hellenic Autonomous Randonneurs (H.A.R.) is a non-profit association, officially the "Autonomous Long-Distance Cyclists of Greece". It's made up of active riders and organizers — old and new, men and women — lovers of long-distance cycling, aiming to give back to the Greek cycling community "the joy, the laughter, the happiness of the journey and companionship, the harmony and the pleasure of pure randonneuring".

Unlike ΛΕ.ΠΟ.Τ.Ε., which operates under the umbrella of the French ACP (Audax Club Parisien), H.A.R. is an independent national body: it follows a "hybrid model", similar to Italy and Germany, certifying the results of its own events itself and maintaining full autonomy over rules, innovations, and direct responsiveness to the community.

Board of Directors: President Elena Zervou (Athens), Vice President Stratos Paisios (Katerini), Secretary Vasilis Oikonomou (Ioannina), Treasurer Giannis Liatsos (Agrinio), Member Giannis Stefanidis (Katerini).
harGuide.topic2ShortDesc: Registration, mandatory equipment, checkpoint controls & homologation
harGuide.topic2Content:
Registration: a one-time registration in the H.A.R. Registry is required, along with an electronic declaration of participation for each brevet separately and acceptance of liability terms. Minors need written guardian consent.

Mandatory equipment: helmet at all times, adequate front/rear lighting for night riding, high-visibility reflective vest, compliance with the Highway Code. Backup lighting is recommended for brevets of 300km+ or in bad weather conditions. A 2-hour penalty applies for riding at night without lights; disqualification if someone starts a night departure without the required equipment.

Checkpoint control: a brevet card stamped at checkpoints; if lost, alternative verification via Strava or photos is accepted, provided it's a single recorded activity.

Time limit: follows the international randonneuring standard per distance (H.A.R. refers to an external calculator for the exact calculation). For routes with total elevation gain over 4,000m, an adjustment applies:
TIME LIMIT = (total actual km / minimum average speed) + time extension.

Homologation: primary verification by the organizer at the finish, secondary verification by the body within one week via photos/GPS, issuing a unique homologation number. Adherence to the route and time limit are considered fundamental rules — any complaints about irregularities are examined case by case.
harGuide.topic3ShortDesc: 200+300+400+600 km certified by H.A.R., within the same year
harGuide.topic3Content:
As with ΛΕ.ΠΟ.Τ.Ε., the Super Randonneur distinction is awarded to anyone who completes, within the same calendar year, all four basic brevets — 200, 300, 400 and 600 km — with valid H.A.R. certification for each one.

The app automatically calculates your H.A.R. SR based on your ride history (the H.A.R. field on each brevet) and displays it on your profile.
harGuide.topic4ShortDesc: Permanent route of 600km+ with 10,000m+ elevation gain, fully autonomous
harGuide.topic4Content:
The Super Randonnée is a permanent route ridden at the participant's own initiative — they choose the date, start time, support strategy and accommodation.

It requires at least 600 km (up to ~620 km) and at least 10,000 m of total elevation gain, usually over mountainous terrain — significantly more demanding physically and mentally than a classic brevet. Support vehicles are completely prohibited; the rider is fully self-supported.

There are two time categories: Tourist (minimum pace of 75 km/day) and Randonneur (60-hour limit). The participant must photograph their bike at designated checkpoints (or get a stamp from a shop) and record the exact times on their personal SR card. After approval, the rider receives a homologation number and is registered on superrandonnees.org — Super Randonnées are not competitive events.
harGuide.topic5ShortDesc: Complete a brevet on your own, any day after the official date
harGuide.topic5Content:
The H.A.R. Rules explicitly provide for (Article 9):
"every cyclist may take part in the brevet of their choice on any day after its official organized date, and as many times as they wish".

The route must be recorded as a single activity, with photographic documentation at checkpoints, exactly as in an official event.

The app already supports this feature: from a brevet's page you can start in Post-ride mode (or Pre-ride, before the official date) and, if the brevet allows it, with a Free Start from any point on the route — as long as you finish where you started.

Also relevant is Article 16.2 "Mini Brevets": routes between 80 and 120 km, with the same homologation standards, which count normally towards the annual Challenge.
harGuide.topic6ShortDesc: 3 categories of yearly distinction: kilometers, elevation, participations
harGuide.topic6Content:
The Challenge is H.A.R.'s annual award institution, with three ranking categories based on the H.A.R. brevets completed within the year:

🥇 The Kilometer Eater — the most total kilometers in H.A.R. brevets
⛰️ The Mountain Charmer — the greatest total elevation gain in H.A.R. brevets
🧭 The Traveler — the most participations in H.A.R. brevets

The winner of each category, in the final ranking at year's end, is awarded by the body with a special prize and gifts.
harGuide.topic7Title: COP Bike Ride — The Greek Leg
harGuide.topic7ShortDesc: Annual global cycling relay; H.A.R. puts Greece on the world map
harGuide.topic7Content:
The "COP Bike Ride" is an ongoing, annually repeated international initiative, aiming to promote proposals for everyday cycling as a tool for reducing carbon emissions, traveling towards the UN Climate Change Conference (COP) each year: it already took place at COP29 (2024) and COP30 (2025, starting from Belém, Brazil), and continues this year towards COP31 in Antalya, Turkey (November 9–20, 2026).

Coordination of the Greek leg for 2026 has been taken on by H.A.R. — effectively putting Greece on the world map of this initiative. The goal is for participation to be a matter for the whole Greek cycling community — clubs, groups and independent riders — without anyone needing to ride the entire route.

The Greek route starts on 9/30 from Athens and arrives on 10/7 at Pınarhisar, Turkey:
9/30 Athens → Atalanti · 10/1 Atalanti → Karditsa · 10/2 Karditsa → Katerini · 10/3 Katerini → Thessaloniki · 10/4 Thessaloniki → Serres · 10/5 Serres → Komotini · 10/6 Komotini → Orestiada · 10/7 Orestiada → Pınarhisar.
